questions.question: If the frequency of a vibrating object is 50 { Hz} , what is its time period?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**0.02 s**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **frequency** of a vibrating object is defined as the total number of oscillations or vibrations it completes in **one second**.
 
• The **time period** (T) is the duration required to complete **one single vibration** or cycle.
 
• There is a fundamental mathematical relationship between these two properties: they are the **reciprocal** of each other. The formula is expressed as **T = 1 / f**, where **f** represents the **frequency**.
 
• Given the data in the question, the **frequency** (f) is **50 Hz**. To find the **time period**, we apply the formula: **T = 1 / 50**.
 
• By performing the division, **1 divided by 50** equals **0.02**. Therefore, the **time period** of the vibrating object is **0.02 s**. ***Hence, the correct answer is 0.02 s.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Frequency and Units:**
 
 
• The **SI unit** of **frequency** is the **Hertz**, abbreviated as **Hz**. It is named after the famous **19th-century** German physicist **Heinrich Rudolf Hertz**, who proved the existence of electromagnetic waves.
 
• A frequency of **1 Hz** means that **one vibration** occurs every **one second**. In this context, **50 Hz** implies that the object is vibrating **50 times** every **one second**.
 
 
 
• **Time Period Characteristics:**
 
 
• The **SI unit** for the **time period** is the **second (s)**.
 
• In wave mechanics, the **time period** remains constant for a stable source, even if the wave travels through different media, provided the source **frequency** does not change.
 
 
 
• **Physical Examples:**
 
 
• **Sound Waves**: The **frequency** of a sound wave determines its **pitch**. A high-frequency vibration produces a **high-pitched** sound (like a whistle), while a low-frequency vibration produces a **low-pitched** sound (like a bass drum).
 
• **Power Supply**: In **India**, the standard **frequency** of the **Alternating Current (AC)** supplied to homes is **50 Hz**, which matches the value provided in this problem.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Inverse Proportion**: The **frequency** and the **time period** are in **inverse proportion**. If the **frequency** of an object doubles, its **time period** is halved.
 
• **Calculation Tip**: To quickly calculate **1/50**, one can multiply both the numerator and the denominator by **2**, resulting in **2/100**, which clearly equals **0.02**.
 
• **Vibratory Motion**: This type of motion is characterized by a "to-and-fro" movement about a central **mean position**. Common examples include the movement of a **simple pendulum**, the prongs of a **tuning fork**, or the strings of a **guitar**.
 
• **Audible Range**: For humans, the audible **frequency** range is typically between **20 Hz** and **20,000 Hz**. Any vibration with a **frequency** below **20 Hz** is called **infrasonic**, and above **20,000 Hz** is called **ultrasonic**.
</ul

questions.question: How can you identify a concave and a convex mirror based on the direction of their reflecting surfaces?

options.text: A concave mirror reflects light outward, while a convex mirror reflects it inward.
Both concave and convex mirrors have the same reflecting surface direction.
A concave mirror and a convex mirror both reflect inward.
A concave mirror has its reflecting surface curved inward; a convex mirror has its reflecting surface curved outward.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**A concave mirror has its reflecting surface curved inward; a convex mirror has its reflecting surface curved outward.**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• A **spherical mirror** is a mirror whose reflecting surface is a part of a hollow sphere of glass. Based on the direction of the curvature of the reflecting surface, they are classified into **concave** and **convex** mirrors.
 
• A **concave mirror** is a spherical mirror whose **reflecting surface is curved inward**, facing towards the **center of the sphere**. It is also known as a **converging mirror** because it converges parallel rays of light after reflection. ***Hence, statement 4 regarding the concave mirror is correct.***
 
• A **convex mirror** is a spherical mirror whose **reflecting surface is curved outward**, facing away from the center of the sphere. It is also known as a **diverging mirror** because it diverges parallel rays of light after reflection. ***Hence, statement 4 regarding the convex mirror is correct.***
 
• Statement 1 suggests a concave mirror reflects light outward; this is incorrect as concave mirrors are **converging**. Statement 2 claims both have the same direction, which is incorrect as they are **opposites**. Statement 3 claims both reflect inward, which is false for **convex mirrors**. ***Hence, statements 1, 2, and 3 are incorrect.***
 
• The identification of these mirrors is fundamental in **optics** for determining the nature of images (real or virtual) and their magnification levels.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Applications of Concave Mirrors:**
 
 
• They are commonly used as **shaving mirrors** or **makeup mirrors** because they can produce an **enlarged and erect image** when the object is placed close.
 
• They are used in **car headlights** and **searchlights** to produce a powerful **parallel beam** of light.
 
• **Dentists** use concave mirrors to see large images of the teeth of patients.
 
• Large concave mirrors are used in **solar furnaces** to focus sunlight for heating purposes.
 
 
 
• **Applications of Convex Mirrors:**
 
 
• They are primarily used as **rear-view mirrors** in vehicles because they always give an **erect (upright) image**, although diminished.
 
• Convex mirrors provide a much **wider field of view** as they are curved outwards, allowing the driver to see a larger area of traffic behind them compared to a plane mirror.
 
• They are used as **security mirrors** in shops and automated teller machines (ATMs) to monitor large areas.
 
 
 
• **Image Formation Characteristics:**
 
 
• **Concave mirrors** can form both **real and inverted** images as well as **virtual and erect** images depending on the position of the object relative to the **focal point**.
 
• **Convex mirrors** always form a **virtual, erect, and diminished** image, regardless of the distance between the object and the mirror.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Principal Terminology:**
 
 
• The center of the reflecting surface of a spherical mirror is called the **Pole (P)**.
 
• The center of the hollow sphere of which the mirror is a part is the **Center of Curvature (C)**.
 
• The distance between the Pole and the Center of Curvature is the **Radius of Curvature (R)**.
 
• The **Principal Focus (F)** is the point on the principal axis where rays parallel to the axis meet (or appear to meet) after reflection.
 
 
 
• **Mathematical Relationship:** For spherical mirrors of small apertures, the **Radius of Curvature (R)** is found to be **twice the focal length (f)**, represented by the formula **R = 2f**.
 
• **Sign Convention:** According to the **New Cartesian Sign Convention**, the focal length of a **concave mirror is negative**, while the focal length of a **convex mirror is positive**.
</ul

questions.question: Why do passengers in a moving car tend to jerk forward when the brakes are suddenly applied?

options.text: Because of the friction between the seat and the body
Due to the force applied by the engine
Because the brakes push the passengers forward
Because of the inertia of motion that keeps the body moving forward

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Because of the inertia of motion that keeps the body moving forward**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The phenomenon of passengers jerking forward is a direct application of **Newton's First Law of Motion**, also known as the **Law of Inertia**.
 
• According to this law, an object continues in its state of **rest** or **uniform motion** in a straight line unless acted upon by an external **unbalanced force**.
 
• When a car is in motion, both the vehicle and the **passengers** possess **Inertia of Motion**, meaning they have a tendency to keep moving at the same speed and in the same direction.
 
• When the **brakes** are applied suddenly, an external **force** stops the car. The lower part of the passenger's body, being in direct contact with the car seat, comes to **rest** along with the car due to **friction**.
 
• However, the **upper part** of the body is not in rigid contact with the car and tries to maintain its state of **motion** due to **inertia**. ***Hence, the body jerks forward as it continues to move while the base has stopped.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Definition of Inertia:** **Inertia** is the inherent property of a body by virtue of which it resists any change in its state of **rest** or **uniform motion**. It is not a force but a fundamental characteristic of **matter**.
 
• **Types of Inertia:**
 
 
• **Inertia of Rest:** The tendency of an object to stay at **rest**. For example, when a bus starts suddenly, passengers jerk **backwards** because the lower body moves forward with the bus while the upper body tries to remain at rest.
 
• **Inertia of Motion:** The tendency of an object to stay in **motion**. This is observed when a moving car stops abruptly, as mentioned in the question.
 
• **Inertia of Direction:** The tendency of an object to maintain its **direction** of travel. For example, when a car takes a sharp **curve**, passengers are thrown to one side because their bodies try to continue moving in the original **straight line**.
 
 
 
• **Relationship with Mass:** The **inertia** of an object is measured by its **mass**. A body with a **larger mass** (like a truck) has more **inertia** and requires a greater **force** to change its state compared to an object with a **smaller mass** (like a bicycle).
 
• **Historical Context:** These principles were first mathematically detailed by **Sir Isaac Newton** in his work **'Philosophiæ Naturalis Principia Mathematica'**, published in the year **1687**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Safety Applications:** The concept of **Inertia of Motion** is the primary reason why **seatbelts** are mandatory in vehicles. Seatbelts provide the necessary **counter-force** to stop the upper body from crashing into the dashboard or windshield during sudden braking or a **collision**.
 
• **Friction's Role:** While **inertia** causes the forward movement, it is the **frictional force** between the person and the seat (and the floor) that eventually helps bring the passenger to a stop relative to the car.
 
• **Galileo’s Contribution:** Before Newton, **Galileo Galilei** was the first to suggest the concept of **inertia** through his experiments with **inclined planes** and falling objects in the early **17th century**.

questions.question: Why are vesicles important in the functioning of the Golgi apparatus?

options.text: They carry materials to and from the Golgi apparatus
They help in forming the nucleus
They generate energy needed for packaging in Golgi apparatus

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**They carry materials to and from the Golgi apparatus**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Golgi apparatus** functions as the central **sorting and dispatching station** for the cell's chemical products. Its primary role involves **modifying, sorting, and packaging** proteins and lipids that are synthesized in the cell.
 
• **Vesicles** are essential components of this system because they act as **transport vehicles**. They fuse with the **cis face** (receiving side) of the Golgi to deliver raw materials from the **Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)**.
 
• Once the materials undergo **biochemical modifications** within the **cisternae** (the flattened sacs of the Golgi), they are pinched off into new **secretory vesicles** from the **trans face** (shipping side).
 
• These vesicles then **carry the processed materials** to their final destinations, such as the **plasma membrane** for secretion outside the cell or to other internal **organelles**. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• Unlike vesicles, **mitochondria** are responsible for **generating energy** (ATP), and **lysosomes** are the organelles that **digest waste** materials. Vesicles do not play a primary role in forming the **nucleus**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

 
• **Discovery**: The Golgi apparatus was discovered by the Italian biologist **Camillo Golgi** in **1898**. He used a unique staining technique called the **black reaction** to visualize it under a microscope.
 
• **Structure**: It consists of a series of **flattened, membrane-bound sacs** known as **cisternae**. A typical Golgi stack may contain anywhere from **three to twenty** cisternae, depending on the cell type.
 
• **Protein Modification**: One of the most important functions of the Golgi is **glycosylation**, where carbohydrate chains are added to proteins to form **glycoproteins**. This process is vital for **cell signaling** and **recognition**.
 
• **Formation of Lysosomes**: The Golgi apparatus is directly involved in the **synthesis of lysosomes**. It packages **hydrolytic enzymes** into specialized vesicles that become the cell's primary **digestive system**.
 
• **Cell Secretion**: In **glandular cells**, the Golgi apparatus is highly developed because these cells are specialized in **secreting substances** like **hormones** and **enzymes**, which require extensive packaging into **secretory vesicles**.
 
• **Plant Cells**: In **plant cells**, the Golgi apparatus is often referred to as **dictyosomes**. They play a crucial role in synthesizing **polysaccharides** like **pectin** and **hemicellulose** used in the construction of the **cell wall**.
</ul

questions.question: What name is given to the flat, stacked sacs that make up the Golgi apparatus?
questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Cisternae**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The **Golgi apparatus** is composed of a series of flattened, **membrane-bound sacs** known as **Cisternae**. These structures are typically stacked together in a parallel fashion, resembling a stack of pancakes. ***Hence, option 1 is correct.***
 
• A typical **Golgi stack** contains anywhere from **4 to 8 cisternae**, although in some **protists**, the number can reach up to **60**. Each **cisterna** creates a separate enclosed environment, allowing for different chemical reactions to occur at different stages of processing.
 
• The **cisternae** are functionally distinct and exhibit **polarity**. The **cis face** is the receiving side located near the **Endoplasmic Reticulum (ER)**, while the **trans face** is the shipping side that faces the **plasma membrane**.
 
• Within these **cisternae**, the cell performs essential **modifications** to **proteins** and **lipids**, such as **glycosylation** (adding sugar chains) and **phosphorylation**.
 
• The **Golgi apparatus** plays a vital role in the **secretory pathway**, acting as the primary center for **sorting** and **packaging** molecules into **vesicles** for delivery to specific **intracellular** or **extracellular** destinations.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Cristae:**
 
 
• These are the internal **infoldings** or finger-like projections of the **inner mitochondrial membrane**.
 
• The primary function of **cristae** is to increase the **surface area** of the **mitochondria**, which facilitates higher rates of **ATP (Adenosine Triphosphate)** production through **cellular respiration**.
 
• They house the **Electron Transport Chain** and the enzyme **ATP synthase**, which are crucial for **energy metabolism**.
 
 
 
• **Vesicles:**
 
 
• These are small, **spherical**, membrane-bound compartments that **transport** or **store** substances within the **cytoplasm**.
 
• In the context of the **Golgi complex**, **transport vesicles** bring materials from the **ER** to the **cis-Golgi**, while **secretory vesicles** bud off from the **trans-Golgi** to carry finished products to the **cell membrane**.
 
 
 
• **Thylakoids:**
 
 
• These are disc-like, membrane-bound structures found inside **chloroplasts** of **plant cells** and **cyanobacteria**.
 
• They are arranged in stacks called **grana** and contain **chlorophyll**, the pigment responsible for capturing **light energy**.
 
• **Thylakoids** are the primary site for the **light-dependent reactions** of **photosynthesis**, where **solar energy** is converted into **chemical energy**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Discovery:** The **Golgi apparatus** was first identified in **1898** by the Italian physician and biologist **Camillo Golgi** using a **silver nitrate** staining technique.
 
• **Cellular Location:** It is found in almost all **eukaryotic cells**, including **plants**, **animals**, and **fungi**, but is absent in **prokaryotic cells** like **bacteria**.
 
• **Analogy:** Because of its role in **sorting**, **tagging**, and **distributing** cellular products, it is frequently referred to as the **"Post Office"** or **"Shipping Center"** of the cell.
 
• **Dictyosomes:** In **plant cells**, the **Golgi stacks** are often referred to as **dictyosomes** and are usually more scattered throughout the **cytoplasm** compared to the centralized Golgi in **animal cells**.
</ul

questions.question: The magnetic field around a straight current-carrying conductor:

options.text: forms concentric circles around the conductor

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**forms concentric circles around the conductor**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The magnetic field produced by a **straight current-carrying conductor** forms a pattern of **concentric circles** centered at every point on the conductor. These circles lie in a plane **perpendicular** to the direction of the current.
 
• The discovery of the relationship between electricity and magnetism was made by **Hans Christian Oersted** in **1820**, when he noticed a compass needle deflect near a metallic wire carrying **electric current**.
 
• The direction of these magnetic field lines can be easily determined using the **Right-Hand Thumb Rule** (also known as **Maxwell’s Corkscrew Rule**). According to this rule, if the **thumb** of the right hand points in the direction of the **current**, the **curled fingers** will indicate the direction of the **magnetic field lines**.
 
• The strength or **magnitude** of the **magnetic field (B)** at any given point is **directly proportional** to the **current (I)** passing through the conductor. If the current increases, the magnetic field becomes stronger.
 
• The magnitude of the **magnetic field** is **inversely proportional** to the **distance (r)** from the conductor. As the distance from the wire increases, the **concentric circles** representing the field lines are drawn further apart, indicating a decrease in field strength.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Right-Hand Thumb Rule Details**: 
 
 
• If the current flows **vertically upwards**, the magnetic field lines appear to move in an **anti-clockwise direction** when viewed from above.
 
• If the current flows **vertically downwards**, the magnetic field lines appear to move in a **clockwise direction**.
 
 
 
• **SI Unit**: The **SI unit** of **magnetic field induction** or magnetic flux density is the **Tesla (T)**, named after the inventor **Nikola Tesla**. Another smaller unit used is the **Gauss (G)**, where **1 Tesla = 10,000 Gauss**.
 
• **Visualization**: The pattern of **concentric circles** can be visualized by passing a straight wire through a horizontal cardboard and sprinkling **iron filings** on it. When current is passed, the filings arrange themselves in circular patterns around the wire.
 
• **Mathematical Expression**: For an infinitely long straight conductor, the magnetic field **B** at a distance **r** is given by the formula **B = (μ₀I) / (2πr)**, where **μ₀** is the **permeability of free space** (approximately **4π × 10⁻⁷ T·m/A**).

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The magnetic field lines are **closed continuous loops**; however, for a straight wire, they simply loop around the wire itself without a defined "North" or "South" pole in the traditional bar-magnet sense.
 
• The field lines **never intersect** each other. If they did, it would mean that at the point of intersection, the **magnetic field** has two different directions, which is physically impossible.

questions.question: Which structural feature contributes to the high reactivity of unsaturated organic compounds?

options.text: Presence of halogen atoms attached to the carbon framework
Total absence of hydrogen atoms within the compound molecule
Incomplete formation of the carbon atom backbone structure
Existence of double or triple bonds between carbon atoms

questions.solution:

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Unsaturated organic compounds** are defined by the presence of **double bonds** or **triple bonds** between **carbon atoms** within their molecular structure.
 
• The high reactivity of these compounds is primarily due to the presence of **pi (π) bonds**. Unlike **sigma (σ) bonds**, which are formed by the head-on overlap of atomic orbitals, **pi bonds** result from the lateral overlap of **p-orbitals**.
 
• These **pi bonds** are characterized by a high **electron density** located above and below the plane of the bonded **carbon atoms**, making the electrons easily accessible to **electrophilic reagents**.
 
• Because these bonds are relatively weaker than **single bonds**, they can be easily broken to form new **single bonds** with other atoms. This allows unsaturated compounds to undergo **addition reactions** readily. ***Hence, option 4 is the correct statement.***
 
• In contrast, **saturated compounds** (alkanes) contain only **single C-C bonds** and are much less reactive because they require **substitution reactions**, which involve breaking stronger **sigma bonds**.

• **Hybridization**: In unsaturated compounds, the **carbon atoms** involved in **double bonds** are **sp2 hybridized**, while those in **triple bonds** are **sp hybridized**. This geometric arrangement contributes to the spatial availability of **electrons** for reactions.
 
• **Functional Groups**: While the presence of **halogen atoms** (Option 1) can increase the reactivity of a molecule, it characterizes **haloalkanes** rather than the inherent nature of **unsaturation**.
 
• **Hydrogen Content**: The **absence of hydrogen** (Option 2) does not define unsaturation; for instance, **Carbon Tetrachloride (CCl4)** has no hydrogen but is a **saturated** molecule because it only contains **single bonds**.

__
 
• The **Law of Constant Proportion**, also known as the **Law of Definite Proportions**, was proposed by the French chemist **Joseph Proust** in **1799**. It states that a chemical compound always contains its component elements in a **fixed ratio by mass**, regardless of its source or method of preparation.
 
• **Mixtures**: A mixture consists of two or more substances physically combined in **any proportion**. Because the components of a mixture do not react chemically to form a new substance with a fixed composition, the **Law of Constant Proportion** is **not applicable** to them. For example, a salt-water solution can have varying amounts of salt. ***Hence, statement 1 is correct.***
 
• **Ionic Compounds**: These are substances formed by the chemical combination of elements through ionic bonds. They follow the **Law of Constant Proportion** strictly. For instance, **Sodium Chloride (NaCl)** always contains **Sodium** and **Chlorine** in a fixed mass ratio of approximately **23:35.5**. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• **Compounds**: By definition, a compound is a substance formed when two or more elements are **chemically bonded** together. Every pure sample of a specific compound will always have the same elements in the same **mass proportion**. Water (**H2O**), for example, always contains **Hydrogen** and **Oxygen** in a **1:8 ratio** by mass. ***Hence, statement 3 is incorrect.***
 
• **Elements**: Elements are pure substances consisting of only **one type of atom**. While the law governs how elements combine to form compounds, it is technically "applicable" in the sense that elements are the constituents that define the proportions in chemical reactions. However, compared to mixtures, they represent the **fundamental units** that obey chemical laws. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Nature of Mixtures**:
 
 
• Mixtures are classified into **Homogeneous** (uniform composition, like air or alloys) and **Heterogeneous** (non-uniform composition, like sand and iron filings).
 
• Unlike compounds, the components of a mixture **retain their original physical properties** and can be separated by physical methods such as **filtration**, **distillation**, or **magnetization**.
 
• The **variable composition** is the defining feature that exempts them from the **Law of Definite Proportions**.
 
 
 
• **Chemical Laws of Combination**:
 
 
• **Law of Conservation of Mass**: Formulated by **Antoine Lavoisier** in **1789**, stating that mass is neither created nor destroyed in a chemical reaction.
 
• **Law of Multiple Proportions**: Proposed by **John Dalton** in **1803**, stating that if two elements form more than one compound, the masses of one element that combine with a fixed mass of the other are in a **ratio of small whole numbers**.
 
 
 
• **Dalton’s Atomic Theory**:
 
 
• In **1808**, **John Dalton** provided the theoretical explanation for these laws. He stated that **atoms** of different elements combine in **simple whole-number ratios** to form compounds.
 
• This theory explains why the **relative number and kinds of atoms** are constant in a given compound, directly supporting **Proust's** findings.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Exceptions to the Law**: While generally true for most inorganic compounds, **Non-stoichiometric compounds** (also called **Berthollides**) do not follow this law. Their elemental composition can vary within certain limits, often found in **solid-state chemistry** and **mineralogy** (e.g., **Ferrous Oxide** often appearing as **Fe0.95O**).
 
• **Isotopes**: The law can also be slightly affected by the presence of **isotopes**. Since isotopes of an element have different **atomic masses**, a compound made with different isotopic ratios will have different mass proportions, even though it is chemically the "same" compound.

questions.question: What happens in the female body if the egg is NOT fertilised?

options.text: The thick uterine lining is retained permanently.
The egg remains in the uterus and turns into an embryo.
The uterine lining breaks down and is expelled as blood and mucous.
The ovary stops releasing eggs permanently.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**The uterine lining breaks down and is expelled as blood and mucous**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• The process in which the female body sheds the lining of the **uterus** when pregnancy does not occur is known as **menstruation**.
 
• If the egg released during **ovulation** is not fertilized by a **sperm**, it lives for about **24 hours** and then begins to degenerate. 
 
• Without fertilization, the **corpus luteum** (a temporary endocrine structure in the ovary) degenerates, leading to a sharp decline in the levels of hormones like **progesterone** and **estrogen**.
 
• The **endometrium** (thick uterine lining), which was prepared to nourish a fertilized egg, is no longer needed. Consequently, this lining breaks down and is discharged through the **vagina** as a mixture of **blood**, **mucous**, and tissue. ***Hence, statement 3 is correct.***
 
• The **thick uterine lining** is not retained permanently; instead, it is rebuilt during every cycle to prepare for a potential pregnancy. ***Hence, statement 1 is incorrect.***
 
• An egg only turns into an **embryo** if it is successfully **fertilized** by a male gamete (sperm). If fertilization does not happen, the egg simply disintegrates. ***Hence, statement 2 is incorrect.***
 
• The **ovary** does not stop releasing eggs permanently after a single unfertilized cycle. This process continues monthly until a woman reaches **menopause**, typically between the **ages of 45 and 55**. ***Hence, statement 4 is incorrect.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **The Menstrual Cycle:** It is the reproductive cycle in female primates (e.g., monkeys, apes, and human beings). The first menstruation begins at puberty and is called **menarche**. It usually repeats at an interval of about **28 to 29 days**.
 
• **Phases of the Cycle:**
 
 
• **Menstrual Phase:** Lasts for **3 to 5 days**, involving the shedding of the **endometrial lining**.
 
• **Follicular Phase:** Primary follicles in the **ovary** grow to become a fully mature **Graafian follicle**, and the **endometrium** regenerates through proliferation.
 
• **Ovulatory Phase:** Occurs around the **14th day** of a 28-day cycle, where a surge in **Luteinizing Hormone (LH)** induces the rupture of the Graafian follicle and the release of the egg.
 
• **Luteal Phase:** The remaining parts of the Graafian follicle transform into the **corpus luteum**, which secretes large amounts of **progesterone**.
 
 
 
• **Hormonal Regulation:** The cycle is regulated by hormones from the **pituitary gland** (**FSH** and **LH**) and the **ovaries** (**estrogen** and **progesterone**). **FSH (Follicle Stimulating Hormone)** stimulates follicular development, while **LH** triggers **ovulation**.
 
• **Menopause:** In human beings, menstrual cycles cease around **50 years** of age; that is termed **menopause**. Cyclic menstruation is an indicator of normal reproductive life and extends between **menarche** and **menopause**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **Fertilization:** If **fertilization** occurs, the **corpus luteum** is maintained and continues to produce **progesterone**, which is essential for maintaining the **endometrium** during **pregnancy**. In this case, the menstrual flow does not occur.
 
• **Lack of Menstruation:** While the absence of a period is often an early sign of **pregnancy**, it can also be caused by other factors such as **stress**, **poor health**, **hormonal imbalances**, or **extreme physical exercise**.
 
• **Zygote Formation:** If the egg is fertilized in the **fallopian tube** (specifically the **ampulla**), it forms a **zygote**, which then undergoes cleavage to become an **embryo** before implanting in the uterine wall.
</ul

Consider the following statements and select the correct option.

Statement B: Farmers use pH values to decide the type of fertiliser to add.

options.text: Both statements A and B are correct.
Statement A is correct but B is incorrect.

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Both statements A and B are correct**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• **Statement A**: Plants require a specific **soil pH** range for healthy development because the availability of **essential nutrients** is directly influenced by the acidity or alkalinity of the soil. Most common crops and garden plants prefer a **slightly acidic to neutral** range, typically between **pH 6.0 and 7.0**. If the pH deviates significantly from this range, nutrients like **Nitrogen**, **Phosphorus**, and **Potassium** may become chemically "locked" and unavailable to the plant roots. ***Hence, statement A is correct.***
 
• **Statement B**: Farmers and gardeners perform **soil testing** to determine the **pH value** before planting. This information is crucial for deciding the **type of fertiliser** or soil conditioner required; for instance, if the soil is too **acidic**, farmers add **lime (calcium carbonate)** to raise the pH, whereas if it is too **alkaline**, they may add **sulfur** or **acidifying fertilisers** like **ammonium sulfate** to lower the pH. ***Hence, statement B is correct.***
 
• The **interaction between soil pH and fertilisers** ensures that the chemical environment of the **rhizosphere** is optimized for **ion exchange**, allowing plants to absorb minerals effectively.
 
• Proper **pH management** prevents **nutrient toxicity** (such as **Aluminum toxicity** in very acidic soils) and **nutrient deficiency** (such as **Iron chlorosis** in alkaline soils).
 
• ***Hence, the correct answer is both statements A and B are correct.***

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Definition of Soil pH**: It is a measure of the **hydrogen ion (H+) concentration** in the soil solution. The scale ranges from **0 to 14**, where **7.0** is neutral, values **below 7.0** are acidic, and values **above 7.0** are alkaline.
 
• **Factors Affecting pH**: Several factors influence soil pH, including **parent material** (the type of rock the soil formed from), **climate** (rainfall causes leaching of basic cations like **Calcium** and **Magnesium**, leading to acidity), and the **decomposition of organic matter**.
 
• **Impact on Microorganisms**: The **biological activity** of soil is also pH-dependent; for example, **Rhizobium bacteria**, which are responsible for **Nitrogen fixation** in leguminous plants, thrive best in **neutral or slightly alkaline** soils and their activity decreases in **acidic environments**.
 
• **Nutrient Availability Trends**: In **acidic soils** (pH below **5.5**), the solubility of **Aluminum**, **Iron**, and **Manganese** increases, which can be toxic to plants. Conversely, in **alkaline soils** (pH above **8.0**), **Phosphorus** often reacts with **Calcium** to form insoluble compounds, making it unavailable to plants.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

For **alkaline soils**, besides elemental **sulfur**, materials like **Gypsum (Calcium Sulfate)** are used to improve soil structure and manage **sodium levels**.
 
• **Logarithmic Scale**: It is important to note that the pH scale is **logarithmic**; a change of **1 unit** on the scale represents a **10-fold** change in acidity or alkalinity. For example, a soil with **pH 5.0** is **10 times** more acidic than a soil with **pH 6.0**.
 
• **Cation Exchange Capacity (CEC)**: The ability of soil to hold and exchange nutrients is often linked to pH. As pH increases, the **CEC** of many soils also increases, allowing the soil to retain more **nutrient cations** like **Potassium (K+)** and **Magnesium (Mg2+)**.
 
• **Fertiliser Choice**: The use of **Urea** and **Ammonium-based fertilisers** can gradually **increase soil acidity** over time due to the process of **nitrification**, which releases **hydrogen ions** into the soil.
</ul

__
 
• **Menstruation** is the natural, cyclic process in human females involving the shedding of the **endometrium** (the inner lining of the **uterus**).
 
• This process occurs specifically when the **ovum** (egg) released during the **ovulation** phase is **not fertilised** by a **sperm**.
 
• In the absence of **fertilisation**, the **corpus luteum** degenerates, leading to a sharp decline in the levels of **progesterone** and **estrogen** hormones.
 
• The lack of these hormones causes the **uterine lining** to break down, resulting in bleeding that exits the body through the **vagina**.
 
• A typical **menstrual flow** lasts for approximately **3 to 7 days**, and the entire **menstrual cycle** repeats roughly every **28 days**, although variations between **21 to 35 days** are considered normal.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

• **Luteal Phase**: The phase following ovulation where the **uterus** prepares for a potential **pregnancy** by thickening its lining.
 
 
 
• **Important Milestones**:
 
 
• **Menarche**: The very first occurrence of **menstruation** in a female, typically happening during **puberty** between the ages of **10 and 15**.
 
• **Menopause**: The biological stage marking the end of **menstrual cycles**, usually diagnosed after a woman has gone **12 months** without a period, typically occurring between the ages of **45 and 55**.
 
 
 
• **Clarification of Other Options**:
 
 
• **Maturation**: This refers to the biological process of **development**. In the reproductive context, it often refers to **oocyte maturation**, where an immature egg develops into a mature one within the **follicle**.
 
• **Fertilisation**: The process where a **sperm** cell fuses with an **egg** cell to form a **zygote**. This usually takes place in the **ampulla** of the **Fallopian tube**.
 
• **Maintenance**: In reproductive biology, this refers to the **maintenance of the endometrium** during **pregnancy**. If the egg is fertilised, the hormone **progesterone** prevents the lining from shedding to support the growing **embryo**.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The cycle is regulated by a complex interplay of hormones from the **hypothalamus**, **pituitary gland**, and the **ovaries**.
 
• The **Endometrium** is highly vascularized (rich in blood vessels) to provide nutrients to a potential **fetus**; its shedding is what causes the **menstrual blood**.
 
• If **pregnancy** occurs, the **menstrual cycle** stops temporarily as the **placenta** begins producing **Human Chorionic Gonadotropin (hCG)** to maintain the **uterine lining**.
</ul

questions.question: Where does the heat energy go when the solid melts but its temperature remains the same?

options.text: It is lost to the surroundings while overcoming the forces of repulsion.
It is used to overcome the forces of attraction between the particles.
It is lost to the surroundings while overcoming the forces of attraction.
It is used to overcome the forces of repulsion between the particles.

questions.solution:
p data-end="57" data-start="0">The correct answer is __**It is used to overcome the forces of attraction between the particles**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• When a **solid** reaches its **melting point**, it begins to transition into a **liquid** state. During this process, even if heat is continuously supplied, the **temperature** of the substance remains **constant** until the entire solid has melted.
 
• This phenomenon occurs because the heat energy supplied is being utilized to change the **state of matter** rather than increasing the **kinetic energy** of the particles.
 
• Specifically, the energy is consumed to break the **intermolecular forces of attraction** that hold the particles in a fixed, rigid position in the **solid lattice**. ***Hence, the statement that it is used to overcome the forces of attraction is correct.***
 
• Since the **average kinetic energy** of the particles does not increase during this phase change, the **thermometer** does not show a rise in **temperature**.
 
• This "hidden" heat that is absorbed by the substance without a change in temperature is known as **Latent Heat**.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Latent Heat of Fusion:**
 
 
• The **Latent Heat of Fusion** is defined as the amount of **heat energy** required to change **1 kg** of a **solid** into a **liquid** at its **melting point** at **atmospheric pressure**.
 
• For example, the latent heat of fusion for **ice** is approximately **3.34 x 10⁵ Joules per kilogram (J/kg)**. This means **3.34 x 10⁵ J** of energy is needed to convert **1 kg** of ice at **0 degree Celsius** to water at **0 degree Celsius**.
 
 
 
• **Melting Point and Pressure:**
 
 
• The **melting point** is the specific **temperature** at which a solid becomes a liquid at **1 atmospheric pressure**. For **ice**, this is **273.15 K** or **0 degree Celsius**.
 
• Different substances have different melting points based on the strength of their **chemical bonds** or **intermolecular forces**. Substances with **stronger forces of attraction** require more energy (higher temperature) to melt.
 
 
 
• **Comparison of Energy Levels:**
 
 
• Particles in **water** at **0 degree Celsius** (273 K) have **more energy** as compared to particles in **ice** at the same **temperature**.
 
• This extra energy is the **latent heat** absorbed during the melting process, which allows the water particles to move more freely than the restricted particles in the ice structure.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• **The Role of Energy in Phase Change:**
 
 
• In **Thermodynamics**, during a phase transition like **melting (fusion)** or **boiling (vaporization)**, the energy supplied goes into increasing the **potential energy** of the system rather than the **kinetic energy**.
 
• Because **temperature** is a measure of the **average kinetic energy**, the temperature remains **stagnant** during the entire duration of the state change.
 
 
 
• **Distinction between Forces:**
 
 
• The options mentioning **forces of repulsion** are scientifically inaccurate in this context. Melting is strictly about overcoming the **attractive forces** (like **Hydrogen bonding** in ice or **Ionic bonds** in salts) that keep the solid intact.
 
• Energy is not "lost" to the **surroundings** during the melting process in an ideal scenario; rather, it is **absorbed** by the substance to perform **work** against the **molecular bonds**.
 
 
</ul

questions.question: For 5 innings, a cricketer has an average of 80 runs. In the 6th inning, he scores 194 runs. His average score increased by _______.

Current average of 5 innings = 80 runs.

Runs scored in the 6th inning = 194.

Extra runs scored above the current average = 194 − 80 = 114 runs.

These extra runs will be distributed equally among all 6 innings.

Increase in average = 114 ÷ 6 = 19 runs.

**∴ The correct answer is 19 runs.**

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/c76c13ba2d2ab46b47f8a931ae621dac081a0cb266b142dc23f58659fac4a466.png] **__Alternate Method__**

**Given:**

Average score for 5 innings = 80 runs

Score in the 6th inning = 194 runs

 Innings 1 to 5 Average = 80 6th Inning Base = 80 Extra = +114 
 
 Distributed over 6 innings = +19 New Average = 80 + 19 = 99 

**Formula Used:**

Average = Total sum of values ÷ Total number of values

**Calculations:**

⇒ Total runs in the first 5 innings = 5 × 80 = 400 runs

⇒ Total runs after the 6th inning = 400 + 194 = 594 runs

⇒ New average after 6 innings = 594 ÷ 6 = 99 runs

⇒ Increase in average = New average − Old average

⇒ Increase in average = 99 − 80 = 19

**∴ The correct answer is 19 runs.**

Similar to the combined average, it assigns a specific weight (w) to each value (x), and the final result is calculated as ∑(w × x) ÷ ∑w.

x = 2, y = 1

 Length = 5 m Area = 15 m² Breadth = 3 m

⇒ Area = (2x)² − (y²)²

questions.question: With which of the following government bodies, did the Reserve Bank of India (RBI) collaborate in June 2025 to curb spam loan and credit‑card calls?

options.text: Securities and Exchange Board of India (SEBI)

questions.solution:
The correct answer is __**Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI)**__.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/36f36cd5ece4186095afcf2ffbfb7b80cc04b6c2e3226e7477a419a9fbc96f85.png] **__Key Points__**

__
 
• In **June 2025**, the **Reserve Bank of India (RBI)** and the **Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI)** entered into a strategic collaboration to tackle the growing menace of **spam calls** and **SMS** related to **unsolicited loan offers** and **credit card** services.
 
• The primary objective of this partnership is to safeguard consumers from **financial fraud** and harassment caused by **unregistered telemarketers** who bypass standard regulatory protocols.
 
• As part of the initiative, the **RBI** issued directives to all **Scheduled Commercial Banks** and **NBFCs** to ensure that their third-party agents strictly adhere to **TRAI’s** guidelines regarding **Unsolicited Commercial Communications (UCC)**.
 
• The collaboration involves the implementation of **AI-driven filters** and **blockchain-based Distributed Ledger Technology (DLT)** to monitor and block **headers** and **templates** used by scammers to impersonate legitimate financial institutions.
 
• This move follows a significant rise in complaints regarding **digital lending apps** and **spam calls** that often lead to **phishing** attacks and unauthorized data harvesting.

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/f13e2ad6582c16aa62a83672e2547ad20a01fddb61962a1acce42eb9a1a99caa.png] **Additional Information__**

__
 
• **Telecom Regulatory Authority of India (TRAI):**
 
 
• Established on **February 20, 1997**, under the **Telecom Regulatory Authority of India Act, 1997**, to regulate telecom services in India.
 
• It is headquartered in **New Delhi** and functions as a **statutory body** to ensure transparency and healthy competition in the telecom sector.
 
• **TRAI** introduced the **Telecom Commercial Communications Customer Preference Regulations (TCCCPR)** in **2018** to provide a framework for controlling **spam** and protecting **subscriber privacy**.
 
 
 
• **Reserve Bank of India (RBI):**
 
 
• The **RBI** was established on **April 1, 1935**, in accordance with the provisions of the **Reserve Bank of India Act, 1934**.
 
• As the **Central Bank** of the country, it regulates the **monetary policy** and oversees the **banking system** to maintain financial stability.
 
• In recent years, the **RBI** has introduced **Digital Lending Guidelines (2022)** to protect borrowers from **predatory lending practices** and **illegal loan apps**.
 
 
 
• **Unsolicited Commercial Communication (UCC):**
 
 
• This refers to any **commercial communication** that a subscriber receives without their **explicit consent**.
 
• The **DND (Do Not Disturb)** registry, managed by **TRAI**, allows users to opt-out of receiving such communications.
 
 

 [IMAGE: https://cdn.repeatermock.com/tb/4f750a2730aad0987b5e719f277ddc90129c657928205c4d3b5aa23049023fa5.png] **Important Points__**

 
• The **Joint Working Group** formed by **RBI** and **TRAI** focuses on technical solutions like **Calling Name Presentation (CNAP)**, which helps users identify the **caller’s identity** before answering.
 
• The **Sanchar Saathi** portal, launched by the **Department of Telecommunications (DoT)**, also plays a crucial role in reporting **fraudulent mobile connections** and **spam**.
 
• Financial institutions found violating these norms face heavy **penalties** under the **Banking Regulation Act, 1949**, and **TRAI** regulations.
 
• This initiative is a critical step toward the **Digital India** vision, ensuring a **secure digital ecosystem** for **online banking** and **financial transactions**.

questions.question: Who was named Sportsperson of the Year with a Disability at the 2025 Laureus Awards?

• **Jiang Yuyan**, a phenomenal **para-swimmer** from **China**, was officially named the **Sportsperson of the Year with a Disability** at the **2025 Laureus World Sports Awards**.

• During the **Paris 2024** games, she won an incredible **seven gold medals**, competing in various individual and relay events within the **S6** and **S7** classifications.

• Born in **2004** in **Shaoxing**, **Zhejiang province**, **China**, she faced significant adversity early in life after losing her right arm and right leg in a car accident at the age of **four**.

• She is widely known by the nickname **"Flying Fish"** due to her extraordinary speed and technique in the swimming pool.

• She began her international career with a breakthrough at the **2019 World Para Swimming Championships** in **London**, where she won **three gold medals** at the age of **14**.

• **The Laureus World Sports Awards:**

• Established in **1999**, these awards are often considered the "Oscars of Sport," honoring the greatest sporting achievements of the previous calendar year.

• The **Sportsperson of the Year with a Disability** category is one of the most prestigious honors in the **Paralympic** movement, highlighting athletes who overcome physical challenges to reach the pinnacle of sport.

• **Laureus Academy:** The final voting body for these awards, the **Laureus World Sports Academy**, consists of **71** of the greatest living sporting legends, ensuring that the winners are recognized by their peers.

questions.question: Dr. C Anandharamakrishnan received the Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar 2024 in the Vigyan Shri category for his contribution to the field of ______.

• Dr. **C Anandharamakrishnan** has been conferred with the prestigious **Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar 2024** in the **Vigyan Shri** category for his pioneering work in **Agricultural Science**.
 
• He currently serves as the **Director** of the **CSIR-National Institute for Interdisciplinary Science and Technology (NIIST)**, located in **Thiruvananthapuram**, **Kerala**.
 
• The **Vigyan Shri** award specifically recognizes individuals who have made distinguished contributions to any field of **science and technology**.

• **Rashtriya Vigyan Puraskar (RVP):**
 
 
• This national award was instituted in **2023** by the **Government of India** to simplify and unify the diverse science awards previously given by various ministries.
 
• It is categorized into four levels: **Vigyan Ratna** (Lifetime Achievement), **Vigyan Shri** (Distinguished Contribution), **Vigyan Yuva-SSB** (Young Scientists), and **Vigyan Team**.
 
• The awards are open to persons of Indian origin (**PIO**) and **non-resident Indians (NRI)**, in addition to citizens of **India**.

• He holds a **Doctoral degree** from **Loughborough University**, **United Kingdom**, and has been instrumental in developing **spray drying** and **electrospraying** techniques for nutrient delivery.
 
• He is a Fellow of the **National Academy of Sciences (NASI)** and the **Royal Society of Chemistry**.

• A total of **33 awards** were announced across various disciplines like **Physics**, **Chemistry**, **Biological Sciences**, and **Mathematics**.

• **Date of Announcement:** The names of the awardees are officially announced on **May 11** every year, which is celebrated as **National Technology Day**.

• **Scientific Impact:** In the field of **Agricultural Science**, Dr. Anandharamakrishnan’s work helps in addressing **food security** and improving the **shelf-life** of agricultural produce through advanced **bioprocessing**.
